title: Faith the seed
hookLine: a brahmin farmer with five hundred plows tells the Buddha to plow for his food
carry: plant one seed you can't see
last: WE PRAISE THE BLESSING OF COMPANIONSHIP.

lines: FIVE HUNDRED PLOWS AT SOWING TIME.
cards: Sowing day on a big farm in Magadha. A brahmin named Kasi Bharadvaja has five hundred plows out in his fields, and at lunchtime he's handing out food to the workers.
A man with a bowl walks up and stands quietly at the edge of the line. The farmer isn't impressed. I plow and I sow, he says, and then I eat.
You should plow and sow too, and then you can eat. It's a fair point, the kind people still make about anyone whose work you can't see. The Buddha's answer is today's poem.

teach.b: The Buddha says: I plow and sow too, brahmin, and then I eat. The farmer is puzzled: we don't see your yoke, your plow, your oxen. So the Buddha describes his farm, in verse.

teach.h: FAITH THE SEED, WISDOM THE PLOW
teach.b: Faith is the seed. Discipline is the rain. Wisdom is my yoke and plow.
Conscience is the pole, the mind the strap, mindfulness my plowshare and goad. Guarded in body and speech, moderate in food. Truth is how I weed.

Effort is my ox, pulling toward freedom without turning back. And this plowing has the deathless as its harvest. Notice where faith sits: it's the seed, the very first thing, put into the ground before anything shows.
Saddha, the Pali word, can be translated faith, trust or confidence. Here it isn't the harvest.

teach.h: TRUST THAT GETS YOU TO BEGIN
teach.b: It's the trust that gets you to begin. Then wisdom and effort and mindfulness do the work. The farmer is moved and offers milk-rice in a bronze bowl.
The Buddha declines: food given in payment for verses isn't for him. In the end the farmer asks to go forth.

A whole collection closed, the oldest poems opened: a snake shedding its skin, a herdsman in the rain, a rhinoceros alone, a friend on the road, and now a field. Each sets an ordinary picture beside a deeper one.

how: Theravada monastics live on alms and do not farm or handle money; lay supporters offer food, and the Kasibharadvaja poem is one text teachers use to explain how monastic and lay life support each other.

o: proof that removes every doubt for good
faith, trust, the confidence to begin
a reward paid out for good deeds

games.q: the Buddha's farm: tap the pairs.

s: the farmer tells the Buddha he should plow and sow before eating
and the Buddha answers that he does plow and sow, in his own way.
in the poem, faith is the harvest
faith is the seed; the harvest is the deathless.
the Buddha accepts the milk-rice as payment for his verses
he declines food given in exchange for reciting verses.

games.q: you're the Buddha, standing with your bowl. the farmer says: I plow and sow, then I eat. you should too. what do you say?
o: I plow and sow too, and then I eat.
games.why: he agrees with the farmer's principle, then shows a farm of faith, wisdom, effort and mindfulness.

practice: Quietly name your own farm: your seed, the small trust that got you started on something good; your plow, the steady tool you use, like patience, honesty or an early alarm; your ox, the effort that keeps pulling.
Then let the breath be the slow work of a field, nothing to force, just showing up.

wordCard.voice: saddha. The Buddha's farming poem: trust is the seed you plant first, then wisdom plows, effort pulls, and the harvest is freedom. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali saddha: faith, trust, confidence. in Sn 1.4, the seed.

carryVoice: Your line: plant one seed you can't see. Trust starts it; wisdom and effort grow it. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sutta Nipata 1.4, Kasibharadvaja Sutta (also Samyutta Nikaya 7.11)
